title: The cut-off king
summary: Win rook and pawn against rook by cutting off the enemy king, counting the files and walking the pawn up to promotion.
part.cut.title: The cut
part.cut.summary: The rook on a file between the black king and the pawn, and the white king climbing with the pawn.
part.count.title: The rule of five
part.count.summary: How many files of cut-off are enough, adding the pawn's rank to the files, and why a single file, with the pawn on the fourth, draws.
part.rank.title: Cutting along a rank
part.rank.summary: The black king kept off the rank in front: the rook goes back and forth and the pawn climbs one square at a time.
part.recap.title: Summary
part.recap.summary: The three rules for your games, the count played once, and the knight pawn exception.
step.t_cut: The pawn is on the fifth rank and your king stands next to it. Black has a simple plan to draw, and you have one move to stop it. What is Black's plan, and which move stops it?
step.t_cut.hint1: Imagine it is Black's turn. Where does the black king want to go?
step.t_cut.hint2: The black king wants to reach d7 and then stand in front of the pawn. There is a file it cannot cross once your rook is on it.
step.cut: 1.Rd1. The rook sits on the d-file, between the black king and the pawn, and the black king can no longer step on it: d8, d7, d6, all forbidden. That is cutting off the king. Now the pawn has a single escort, your king, and the black king watches from far away. Almost every win in rook and pawn against rook starts like this: before you push the pawn, lock the enemy king on the other side of a file. Notice that the rook does not protect the pawn: the king looks after it. The rook's job is to hold the black king back, and that is worth more.
step.late: See why it was urgent. Same position, but Black to move: 1...Kd7. Now the black king goes to e8 or e7, in front of the pawn, and your rook is too late. With the defending king in front of the pawn, the Philidor defence is at hand, and it is a draw. The cut is worth gold, but only to whoever gets there first.
step.d_cut: With the black king cut off, the rest is patience. Watch the white king climb with the pawn beside it.
step.d_cut.m1: 1...Re8. The black rook stands in front of the pawn. It cannot stop the pawn alone, but it will try to bother the king with checks.
step.d_cut.m2: 2.Kf5. The king climbs on the side of the pawn away from the black king.
step.d_cut.m3: 2...Rf8+. Check. The black rook will give every check it can.
step.d_cut.m4: 3.Kg5. The king steps out of check without leaving the pawn. No hurry.
step.d_cut.m5: 3...Re8. The rook goes back in front of the pawn and waits.
step.d_cut.m7: 4...Rf8+. One more check, but now the white king has an answer that attacks the rook.
step.d_cut.m8: 5.Ke7! The king steps in front of the pawn and attacks the rook on f8 as well. The black rook has to leave. From here the pawn climbs with the king beside it, and the black king stays on the other side of the d-file.
step.m_cut: Your turn. Cut off the black king and start climbing with your king next to the pawn.
step.m_cut.hint: 1.Rd1 first. Then the king climbs along the f-file, on the side away from the black king.
step.m_cut.done: That is the rhythm: the cut first, then the king climbs, stepping out of the checks without leaving the pawn.
step.t_count: Now the pawn is on the fourth rank, one square further back than in the last chapter. Cutting off the black king is the right idea, but only one of two cuts wins: along the c-file or along the d-file. Which one?
step.t_count.hint1: Count how many files lie between the black king and the pawn after each cut.
step.t_count.hint2: With the rook on d1 the black king reaches c5, one file from the pawn. With the rook on c1 it stays two files away. Add the pawn's rank to that number.
step.five: In the last chapter the pawn was on the fifth, and one file of cut-off was enough. With the pawn on the fourth you have to count. 1.Rc1. There is a count the textbooks call the rule of five: add the rank the pawn stands on to the number of files separating the defending king from the pawn's file. More than five usually wins; five or less usually draws. Here the pawn is on the fourth rank. With the rook on c1 the black king is two files away: four plus two, six. A win. It is a rule of thumb, with exceptions, but it is right in most positions.
step.d_five: Now with two files of cut-off, in the classic rule of five example, from the books by Soltis and Mednis: a d-pawn on the fourth and the black king on g5, two files away. Watch how the white king escapes the checks from the front.
step.d_five.m1: 1.Kc4. The king climbs on the side away from the black king, the c-file.
step.d_five.m2: 1...Rc8+. The check from the front, which you already know.
step.d_five.m3: 2.Kb5! The king goes to the b-file. That is why the far side needs room: the king uses two files to escape the checks.
step.d_five.m4: 2...Rd8. The rook attacks the pawn, left on its own.
step.d_five.m5: 3.Kc5. The king comes back, defends the pawn and is one rank higher already. After 3...Rc8+ 4.Kb6, the white rook can leave the cut to protect the pawn: the black king is too far away to come back.
step.m_five: Your turn, in the position from the start of this chapter. Pick the right file for the cut and start climbing with the king.
step.m_five.hint: 1.Rc1, the two-file cut. Then the king climbs on the far side: 2.Kf4.
step.m_five.done: Two files of cut-off with the pawn on the fourth: six in the count, and the win is secure. Now it is just the technique you saw.
step.t_rank: Until now the rook cut off along a file. Now it cuts off along a rank: the rook on c5 keeps the black king off the fifth rank and off the c-file. How do the king and pawn climb without losing that cut?
step.t_rank.hint1: The white king has to climb, and for that it needs a path where the black rook cannot bother it. Where can your rook protect it?
step.t_rank.hint2: The rook does not have to stay on the c-file all the time: it can step aside to clear the way for the king and come back later, with check.
step.rank: What changes: the black king is not far away, it is on the same rank as the pawn, and what holds it is a rank, not a file. With the rook on c5, the black king cannot enter the fifth rank: it cannot get in front of the pawn. When the black king is on the pawn's rank, as here, it is called a perfect cut, and it wins with a knight or bishop pawn on any rank. The technique is a staircase: the rook goes back and forth between the a-file and the c-file, and with each round the king and pawn climb one rank. It is a position from Jesús de la Villa's endgame book.
step.d_rank: Watch one full step of the staircase.
step.d_rank.m1: 1.Rc6, and not 1.Ra5?, which offers a trade: after 1...Rxa5 2.bxa5 a rook pawn is left, and it is a draw. The rook moves up one square and stays on the c-file, holding the black king on the other side.
step.d_rank.m2: 1...Rb8. The black rook stands in front of the pawn on the b-file, ready to check from the front when the white king leaves it.
step.d_rank.m3: 2.Ra6! The rook moves to the a-file. Now the white king can climb along the a-file without a check from the front: the rook is there, blocking.
step.d_rank.m4: 2...Kd5. With the rook off the c-file, the black king comes closer.
step.d_rank.m5: 3.Ka4! The king climbs, right next to the pawn.
step.d_rank.m6: 3...Kc4. The black king closes in, hoping to get in front of the pawn.
step.d_rank.m7: 4.Rc6+! The rook returns to the c-file with check and pushes the black king away.
step.d_rank.m8: 4...Kd5. The black king has to leave the c-file and moves away from the pawn. From d5 it attacks the rook on c6.
step.d_rank.m9: 5.b5. The pawn climbs one square, protected by the king, and protects the rook on c6. It is the picture from the start, one rank higher.
step.m_rank: This is the position a few moves later: pawn on b5, king on b4 and the black rook back on b8. It is the picture from the start, one rank higher. Climb one more step of the staircase.
step.m_rank.hint: 1.Rc7 and 2.Ra7; the king climbs with 3.Ka5, the rook comes back with 4.Rc7+ and the pawn advances with 5.b6.
step.m_rank.done: One more step. One more like it and the pawn reaches the seventh, with the black king still on the wrong side: from there comes the Lucena.
step.recap: Take three rules with you. One: cut off the enemy king before you push the pawn, even if the rook lets go of the pawn. Two: count. The pawn's rank plus the files in between, from the enemy king to the pawn; more than five usually wins. And count with the pawn where it will be when the rook arrives. Three: with a cut along a rank, the staircase, the rook going back and forth and the king climbing right next to the pawn; and if the cut is imperfect, whoever moves first decides.
step.exceptions: The rule of five has exceptions, and the best known is this one, by Chéron, from 1923: a knight pawn on the fourth and the black king two files away. The count says six, but it is a draw. The knight pawn leaves the white king only one file, the a-file, to escape the checks from the front, and that is not enough. A rule of thumb helps you think, but the position decides. And the rook pawn asks for even more, as you saw in the Lucena lesson: the black king cut off far away, four files from the pawn or more, so that your rook has time to reach the b-file and open the way out for the king.
step.finish: Now the practical challenge. The black king is already cut off, three files from the bishop pawn. Climb with the king, escape the checks on the far side and reach the Lucena.
ex.e05: Your rook keeps the black king away from the front of the pawn. Climb one step of the staircase. Find the winning move.
ex.e05.hint: Your rook is already on the b-file, guarding the king's path. First the king climbs; then the rook comes back with check.
ex.e05.solution: 1.Kb4, right next to the pawn, and after 1...Kd4, 2.Rd6+: the rook returns with check and pushes the black king away. Then the pawn climbs one square.
ex.e09: A position by Capablanca: the black king is two files from the bishop pawn, but the pawn is still on the second rank. Only one move wins.
ex.e09.hint: Do the count for each possible pawn advance.
ex.e09.solution: 1.f4! The pawn reaches the fourth in one move, and four plus two is six. With 1.f3 the count would be five, and Black would have time to set up the checks from the front. After 1...Re8+, the king climbs with 2.Kf3.
key.cut: The black king is one file away from the pawn. The white rook has to close that file right now, before he gets there: only that move wins.
key.count: Choosing the file to cut on: with the black king two files away from the pawn White wins; with only one, it is a draw.
key.five: The classic example of the rule of five: add the pawn's rank to the number of files between it and the black king. More than five, and White wins.
key.villa: Here the black king is cut off along a rank, not a file. The pawn climbs up protected by rook and king, like going up a staircase.
key.cheron: Chéron, 1923: with a knight pawn, even with the black king two files away, it is a draw. Near the edge there is no room for the white king to hide from the checks.
key.capablanca: Capablanca: the pawn has to advance at once, before the black rook gets in front of it to give checks. One tempo decides.
history: With rook and pawn against rook, the first thing to do is cut off the enemy king: the rook closes a file or a rank, and the king on the other side cannot come back to defend. It is the oldest idea in rook endings, and it leads straight to the Lucena position, which wins. It looks simple, but one file fewer or one tempo more changes the result, which is why authors came up with counting rules such as the rule of five, found in the books of Andrew Soltis and Edmar Mednis. André Chéron showed an exception near the edge in 1923, and Capablanca left an example of how a single tempo decides everything. The theme comes up all the time in master play: in 1978, in Niksic, Boris Gulko had a win like this in his hands against Wolfgang Uhlmann, let it slip with a king move and only won because his opponent went wrong soon after; in 1997, at the British Championship, Chris Ward beat Malcolm Pein by leaving his pawn unprotected to cut off the enemy king. It all fits in one sentence: cut first, count second.
practice: Now the practical challenge: rook and pawn against rook, with the black king far from the pawn. Keep its king away, climb with yours and take the pawn all the way to promotion.
ex.e11: From the game Pein–Ward, British Championship 1997, with the colours swapped. The black rook cuts your king off along the fourth rank. What is the plan? Find the winning move.
ex.e11.hint: The black king is heading for the pawn. Before pushing or bringing your king, ask which file it has to cross.
ex.e11.solution: 1.Re7! The rook leaves the back of the pawn and cuts the black king off along the e-file. (1.Rc6 also wins.) Pushing at once (1.c6), bringing the king (1.Kc3, 1.Kd2) or cutting too close (1.Rd7) gives the black king time to reach the d-file, and it is a draw. After 1...Kf6, the rook steps back along the same file with 2.Re2 (or 2.Re1, 2.Re8): the cut stays, and the white king has all the time it needs to climb.
ex.e14: An imperfect cut: the black king is one rank above the pawn, and the black rook is already in front of it. Only one move wins.
ex.e14.hint: Take the file next to the pawn before Black gets organised. But think about which piece does it without opening a path for the black rook.
ex.e14.solution: 1.Kc4! The king takes the file next to the pawn and protects d4 and d5. With 1.Rc6? the rook would hand the a-file to the black rook: 1...Ra8!, and the side checks (2.Kc4 Ra4+) keep your king from staying with the pawn. And 1.Kc3? stays one rank too low: 1...Ke4 attacks the pawn and draws. After 1...Ke4, 2.Re6+! is the only move: the check drives the black king away from the pawn, and the pawn climbs protected by the king, with 3.d5.
ex.e13: From the game Uhlmann–Gulko, Niksic 1978, with the colours swapped. The black king is far away, but the black rook watches the pawn. Only one path wins, and it has three only moves. Find the winning move.
ex.e13.hint: First force the black rook to stand in front of the pawn. Then use your rook to cut the black king off along a rank, not a file.
ex.e13.solution: 1.e7!, and the black rook has to go to e8. Now 2.Re6! The rook guards the pawn from behind and cuts the black king off along the sixth rank, far from f7. After 2...Kg5, 3.Ke4! is the only move: the king climbs through the centre, right next to the rook. From there it is the staircase along the e-file: the rook steps down one square (4.Re5) when the black king comes close, and the white king goes ahead of it until it reaches the pawn.
part.tempo.title: The pawn's tempo
part.tempo.summary: Count with the pawn where it will be: push it before the black rook gets in front of it.
part.imperfect.title: The imperfect cut
part.imperfect.summary: With the black king one rank above the pawn, whoever moves first decides.
part.behind.title: Rook behind the pawn
part.behind.summary: With the pawn on the seventh, the rook stays behind it and cuts the black king off along a rank. Uhlmann against Gulko, 1978.
step.d_oneFile: And with 1.Rd1? The black king comes to c5, just one file from the pawn: four plus one, five. Watch what happens after 1...Kc5, when the white king tries to climb.
step.d_oneFile.m1: 2.Kf4. The king tries to climb next to the pawn, on the side away from the black king.
step.d_oneFile.m2: 2...Rf8+. A check from the front, along the f-file. The black rook is far from the white king and can check as much as it likes.
step.d_oneFile.m3: 3.Kg5. The king gets out of check, but moves away from the pawn.
step.d_oneFile.m4: 3...Re8. The rook returns to the front of the pawn. Now 4.e5? loses the pawn: 4...Rxe5+.
step.d_oneFile.m5: 4.Kf5. The king comes back to protect the pawn.
step.d_oneFile.m6: 4...Rf8+. And it all repeats. The white king has nowhere to escape the checks without leaving the pawn, because the black king waits on the other side, on c5. This is the frontal defence, the subject of a lesson of its own. With one file of cut-off and the pawn on the fourth, it is a draw.
step.t_tempo: The cut is already made: your rook on c1 keeps the black king two files from the pawn. But the pawn is on the third rank, and three plus two makes five. The black rook, on h8, has not reached the front of the pawn yet. What do you do before it gets there?
step.t_tempo.hint1: Think about what goes into the rule of five, and what one move of yours can change in it.
step.t_tempo.hint2: The black rook needs one move to reach the e-file. Whoever gets there first makes the count work.
step.tempo: 1.e4! The pawn reaches the fourth before the black rook gets in front of it. Now the count is four plus two, six, the same as in the last chapter. The rule of five is counted with the pawn where it will be when the rook arrives. Capablanca left a famous example of this race, where a single pawn tempo decides the ending.
step.d_tempoLate: And if the king climbs first? Watch what happens after 1.Kf4? Rf8+, when the black rook gains, with the check, the tempo it needed.
step.d_tempoLate.m1: 2.Kg4. The king gets out of check and moves away from the pawn.
step.d_tempoLate.m2: 2...Re8! The rook has reached the front of the pawn. Now 3.e4? loses the pawn: 3...Rxe4+.
step.d_tempoLate.m3: 3.Kf4. The king comes back near the pawn.
step.d_tempoLate.m4: 3...Rf8+. And it all repeats: the black rook is in front of the pawn, and the pawn is still on the third. One lost tempo cost the win.
step.m_tempo: Now you, in the position from the start of this chapter. Win the race against the black rook and then climb with the king.
step.m_tempo.hint: The pawn first: it reaches the fourth before the black rook reaches the e-file.
step.m_tempo.done: Pawn on the fourth and two files of cut-off: six in the count. From here it is the technique of the last chapter, with the king climbing on the far side.
step.t_imperfect: Your rook cuts the black king off along the fifth rank, but the black king is on the fourth, one rank above the pawn: the cut is imperfect. The black rook is on f8, in front of the pawn. Which move do you play before Black gets organised?
step.t_imperfect.hint1: Think about what Black would do if it were Black's turn.
step.t_imperfect.hint2: A black rook on the file next to the pawn would stop your king from climbing beside it.
step.imperfect: 1.Kg3! (1.Rg5 also works.) The king takes the g-file, next to the pawn, before the black rook does. In the last chapter the black king was on the pawn's rank, and the cut was perfect. Here it is one rank above, and whoever moves first decides: if the black rook reaches the file next to the pawn, it is a draw. When both moves work, prefer the king: the rook stays on the cut and does not open a file for the black rook.
step.d_imperfect: Now the same position with Black to move. The rook gets there first: after 1...Rg8!, it stands on the file next to the pawn, and the white king can no longer go to g3. Watch what is left for White.
step.d_imperfect.m1: 2.f4. Without the king beside it, the pawn climbs alone.
step.d_imperfect.m2: 2...Ke4! The only move that holds: the black king comes up to the pawn and attacks it. The cut along the fifth does not help: the black king is already on this side of it.
step.d_imperfect.m3: 3.f5. The pawn runs ahead, where the black king cannot reach it.
step.d_imperfect.m4: 3...Rg4. The rook gets ready to attack the pawn from behind, along the f-file.
step.d_imperfect.m5: 4.f6. The pawn reaches the sixth, but the white king was left behind, on f2.
step.d_imperfect.m6: 4...Rf4+. Check, and the rook stands behind the pawn, with the white king far from it. It is a draw.
step.m_imperfect: Now you, with White to move. Get to the file next to the pawn first and climb with the king.
step.m_imperfect.hint: The king takes the g-file before the black rook. After the check, it climbs next to the pawn.
step.m_imperfect.done: 2.Kf4. The king is next to the pawn and the cut along the fifth still stands: from here king and pawn climb together.
step.t_behind: Until now the rook cut off from beside the pawn. Now it stays behind it. The pawn is already on the seventh, the black rook is in front of it and yours is behind it, on d1. Both kings are far away, but if the black king gets close to the pawn, it captures it. How do you close the black king's path without letting go of the pawn?
step.t_behind.hint1: Your rook can cut the black king off along a rank without leaving the d-file.
step.t_behind.hint2: The black king is on the fourth rank. What is the first rank it has to cross to climb?
step.behind: 1.Rd5! The rook stays behind the pawn, protecting it along the file, and closes the fifth rank, the first one the black king has to cross. With 1.Rd6?, the fifth is open: after 1...Kg5, the black king climbs along it to e5, attacks the rook and then reaches the pawn. And 1.Rd4+? only pushes the black king onto the fifth, where it wants to go.
step.d_behind: Watch the white king climb on the far side while the rook holds the cut.
step.d_behind.m1: 1.Rd5! The rook closes the fifth rank without leaving its place behind the pawn.
step.d_behind.m2: 1...Kg3. The black king looks for a way round underneath, along the third rank.
step.d_behind.m3: 2.Kd2. The white king heads for the queenside, away from the black king: the way to the pawn runs along the c- and b-files.
step.d_behind.m4: 2...Kf3. The black king comes closer along the third rank.
step.d_behind.m5: 3.Kc3. The king climbs via the c- and b-files, heading for c5 and c7. The black rook cannot leave d8, and the black king cannot get past the fourth rank.
step.uhlmannGulko: This position comes from a real game: Wolfgang Uhlmann, with White, against Boris Gulko, in Niksic, in the former Yugoslavia, in 1978. After the other pieces were traded, they reached this rook ending. Black, Gulko, has the pawn on e3 and the rook on e6, behind it, and the white king went off to capture the pawn on h4, far from the action. One move earlier, Gulko had a winning path, with the idea of this chapter: cut the enemy king off along a rank with the rook behind the pawn. He played 57...Kf5? and let the white king come back. Uhlmann found the only move that held, 58.Kg3!, but three moves later he went wrong: with 61.Rb3?, when only 61.Rb2 drew, he handed the win back, and Black won. In the final test you will look for the path Gulko missed.
step.m_behind: Now you, in the position from the start of this chapter. Close the black king's path and start bringing your own king.
step.m_behind.hint: The rook stays on the d-file and closes the rank just above the black king. Then the king goes round on the far side.
step.m_behind.done: A cut along the rank, with the rook behind the pawn: the pawn is protected and the black king cannot get through.
key.gulko: Uhlmann against Gulko, Niksic, 1978. One move earlier, Black was winning with the advanced pawn and the rook behind it, but let the win slip. Soon after, White went wrong too, and Black won.
step.m_recap: Now you practise the count. The pawn is on the fourth and the black king on f5. Choose the file for the cut.
step.m_recap.hint: Count the files in between for each cut: with the rook on the d-file, how far does the black king get?
step.m_recap.done: The cut on the e-file leaves two files, d and e, between the black king and the pawn: four plus two, six. On the d-file, the black king would reach the e-file, and it would be four plus one, five.
step.d_cheron: Watch why the count fails here.
step.d_cheron.m1: 1.Rd4. The rook protects the pawn along the fourth rank and keeps cutting the black king off on the d-file.
step.d_cheron.m2: 1...Ke5! The only move that holds: the black king comes right up to the cut and attacks the rook.
step.d_cheron.m3: 2.Kc3. The white king protects the rook and tries to climb along the c-file.
step.d_cheron.m4: 2...Rc8+. A check from the front: the white king cannot stay on the c-file.
step.d_cheron.m5: 3.Rc4. The rook blocks the check, but now it cuts along the c-file, just one file.
step.d_cheron.m6: 3...Rb8! The black rook goes back in front of the pawn. On the other side, the white king only has the a-file to escape the checks, and that is too little. It is a draw.
